title: India Is Selling Its Deadliest Weapons to the Gulf. The UAE Is First in Line.
excerpt: After the Iran war exposed the Gulf's dependence on American military hardware, the UAE is in talks to buy India's supersonic BrahMos missile and its AI-powered Akashteer air defence system — a deal that would reshape defence alignments across the Middle East.
body:
When Iranian ballistic missiles struck targets across the Gulf during the US-Iran war earlier this year, a calculation changed across the Arabian Peninsula. The attack proved that American military presence — air bases, carrier groups, Patriot batteries — was not, by itself, a guarantee of security. Gulf states needed to diversify their suppliers. Fast.

Now, according to four sources cited by Reuters, the United Arab Emirates is in active talks with India to buy two of its most prized defence systems: the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile and the Akashteer AI-enabled air defence platform. The discussions, described as being at "initial stages" but "progressing rapidly," represent one of the most significant Indian arms export negotiations to date.

## What India Is Selling

The BrahMos is not just a missile; it is a calling card. Jointly developed by India's DRDO and Russia's NPO Mashinostroyenia, it flies at Mach 2.8 to 3 — nearly three times the speed of sound — with a 200–300 kg warhead. It can be launched from land, sea, air, and submarines. Its fire-and-forget guidance and low radar cross-section make it exceptionally difficult to intercept. Only the Philippines had previously purchased it, in 2022.

Akashteer, meanwhile, is the kind of system the Gulf war proved essential. Developed by Bharat Electronics and the Indian Army, it is a fully automated, AI-powered air defence control system that integrates radar networks, ISRO satellite data, and battlefield processors into a single platform capable of detecting, tracking, and neutralising drones, missiles, and aircraft in real time.

## Why the UAE Is Looking East

The UAE already possesses formidable American hardware — THAAD and Patriot missile defence systems, MGM-168 ATACMS ballistic missiles. But the Iran war laid bare a vulnerability: a single-supplier dependency in a region where threats can emerge faster than diplomatic channels can respond.

"A diversified supplier base gives the UAE more strategic autonomy, and closer ties with India have the added benefit of not antagonising the US, as the countries remain allies," said Pearl Pandya, South Asia senior analyst at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project.

According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the US supplied 54 per cent of all arms imports to the Middle East between 2021 and 2025, followed by Italy at 12 per cent and France at 11 per cent. India barely registered. That is changing.

## Operation Sindoor Changed the Equation

India's brief but decisive four-day conflict with Pakistan last year, during which it deployed BrahMos and other indigenous systems in combat for the first time, dramatically boosted international interest. Since then, India has signed deals to sell BrahMos to Vietnam and Indonesia, and has fielded enquiries from Thailand, South Africa, Brazil, and Chile.

India's defence exports surged to over $4 billion in the fiscal year ending March 2026 — up from just $7.26 million in 2013–14. The transformation from the world's second-largest arms importer to a credible exporter has been swift, and the UAE deal, if it materialises, would mark its entry into the Middle East's lucrative defence market.

Before any BrahMos sale to the UAE can proceed, India would need Russia's approval, as the missile is jointly developed. One source told Reuters this is unlikely to be a hurdle, given Moscow's close ties with Abu Dhabi.

## The Pakistan Factor

The timing is not accidental. Earlier this year, Saudi Arabia signed a defence cooperation memorandum with Pakistan worth more than $35 billion. India views its deepening partnership with the UAE, in part, as a counterbalance to the Saudi-Pakistan defence axis — a shift in alignment that two Indian government sources acknowledged to Reuters.

The two countries have been building toward this. India and the UAE signed a pact to jointly develop military hardware in recent years, alongside a flurry of trade and energy deals. The defence talks are the latest and most concrete expression of a strategic convergence that has been accelerating since the Gulf war.

## Why the Diaspora Should Watch This Closely

More than 3.5 million Indians live in the UAE — the single largest expatriate community in any country. Gulf security is not an abstract geopolitical concept for the diaspora; it is a matter of personal safety, economic stability, and the viability of the remittance corridor that sends billions of dollars back to India every year.

India selling its own defence systems to protect the Gulf is a reversal that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago. It signals not just a commercial transaction, but a deeper strategic entanglement between India and the region where its largest overseas population lives and works.
